1: Welcome everyone. Introduce yourself briefly. Mention the chess engine demo comes at the end.
2:
During the last 6 months I've worked on different private AI projects.

The first reason is personal: I wanted to take back the joy of developing. As the AI releases got better and better this year, that feeling had kind of got lost. So I wanted to create applications I could never have developed before.

I also wanted answers to a few questions:
• Can a real app or game be built with AI?
• Will a larger project drift: does it stay scalable and stable, or get sloppy over time?
• How much supervision does it need?
• And personally: how can I become a better prompt programmer?

First I built a chess engine, then a jetpack multiplayer 2D platform retro game. Then a 3D first-person, six-degrees-of-freedom sci-fi game, inspired by Descent, which I played a lot in the 90s.
3: Spoiler first: here's what I found. The rest of the talk shows where these come from.
4:
Started coding as a kid in the 80s.

Before going professional in 2001, I spent a few years as a math and chemistry teacher. That taught me to explain things simply, which helps when prompting AI as well.

Since then: product companies, med tech and consulting. I came to SEB two and a half years ago and have been a developer in the HULT team since.

Programming has always been my hobby too. I've spent far too many hours improving my chess engines over the years.

Personal: two grown daughters, and I got married this spring.
5:
My first chess engine was in VB.net. It never made a good move, but I just wanted to see if I could do it. I didn't give up: I read up on the theory and the pseudocode.

The goal: get ranked on CCRL, the site that rates computer chess engines, at 2000 Elo.

Quick note on Elo: it's a rating where the gap between two players predicts the result. 200 points stronger means you score roughly 75%. A beginner is around 800, a strong club player around 2000, and grandmasters start at about 2500.

Second attempt, in C#: better moves, but too slow. A few years later, the third attempt in plain C was about 40 times faster. That's ChessMatrix: Elo 1863, around place 700 on CCRL. Close to the goal, but not quite there.

This summer I built ZeroG with Antigravity and Gemini 3.6 Flash. I broke the work into small steps, the same ones I'd take if I wrote it myself. Everything was unit tested, performance tested and refactored. No change was committed without passing a gate: 400 games against the previous version, with a significant improvement.

Result: Elo 2666, place 398 on CCRL. Over 800 Elo stronger than years of my own work. That's when I realised how incredibly helpful AI can be.

Interesting: it rarely got things wrong, because everything was covered by unit tests. As the engine got stronger, the problem changed. The AI's changes simply stopped improving its strength. The gate rejected them, not because they were buggy, but because they didn't make it play better.

One moment that impressed me: at one point the engine started playing invalid moves. That kind of bug always used to be a nightmare for me, because the search functions are long, complicated and recursive. The AI worked at it for a long time, debugging step by step, and pinpointed the exact error.

Ties back to the findings: small sub-tasks, guiding the AI, and tests plus the 400-game gate as the review. That's what made it work.
6:
Quick look under the hood. The first job of any engine is move generation: list every legal move.

The board is doing exactly that now: from the start position it makes and unmakes each of White's 20 moves. That's depth 1.

Click Depth 2: for each of White's 20 moves, Black has 20 replies. 400 positions.

Click Depth 3: 8,902 positions. Point at the table: depth 6 is already 119 million. It grows roughly 30 times per move. Engines generate millions of positions per second, and it still isn't enough to look at everything.

That's why move generation has to be fast and exactly right. One wrong move in here and the whole search is wrong. This is where unit tests saved me, and where the AI's step-by-step debugging impressed me.
7:
Since we can't look at everything, the engine has to be smart about what it looks at.

• Search ahead: I pick the move best for me, and assume my opponent picks the move best for them. That's minimax.
• Prune: skip lines that can't change the answer. That's alpha-beta.
• Evaluate the position at the end of each line: material, piece placement, king safety.

Walk the tree: on the left, the opponent's best reply leaves me at 3. On the right, the first reply already gives me only 2. Since 2 is worse than the 3 I already have, I don't need to look at the other replies. That's the pruning, and it's why engines can search so deep.

Note: this kind of 'AI' is search plus a scoring function, not a language model. The language model helped me write it.

Simple to describe, very hard to make fast and correct. That's where the AI helped, and where the 400-game gate mattered.
8:
Alpha-beta is just the start. There are many, many more pruning techniques, and you need them to make the search strong. Three examples:

• Null move pruning: let the opponent move twice in a row. If I'm still clearly winning even after giving away a free move, this position is so good that I don't need to search it fully.
• Late move reductions: moves are sorted so the most promising ones come first. Moves late in the list are searched less deeply. If one surprises us, we search it again at full depth.
• Futility pruning: close to the end of the search, if I'm far behind and a quiet move can't possibly make up the difference, skip it.

Each one is a trade-off: search less, risk missing something. Only the 400-game gate tells you if it's worth it.

The evaluation is just as important. A deep search with a bad evaluation still picks bad moves. In the past evaluation was hand-written: material, piece placement, king safety, with weights tuned by hand.

Nowadays evaluation is done with a trained neural network, called NNUE. It's trained on millions of positions and is designed to update quickly as moves are made, so it's fast enough to run inside the search. That was one of the biggest jumps in engine strength in recent years.
9:
One thing I learned while building ZeroG: performance is everything in a chess engine. The faster the search, the deeper it sees in the same time, and the stronger it plays.

So I asked the AI to set up benchmarking: small programs that run move generation, search and the neural network on fixed positions and measure the speed. On top of that, a profiler. On the Mac it's the built-in 'sample' tool, which checks a thousand times a second which function the program is in. On Linux it uses Valgrind's Callgrind. It's all one command: make profile.

Then the nice part: I let the AI read the profiler output itself. It's a long text report of call stacks and sample counts. Tedious for me, easy for the AI. It quickly pointed out the hot spots, fixed them, re-ran the benchmark and confirmed the speed-up.

I even saved the workflow as a skill, so the AI knows how to profile the engine next time.

Takeaway: give the AI a way to measure. With hard numbers it can find and fix problems on its own, and prove the fix worked.
10:
I want to stress one thing about the chess engine: the improvement is not a feeling. It's measured.

A lot of talk about AI productivity is gut feeling: 'it feels faster', 'the code seems better'. That's hard to prove.

Chess engines are different. Elo comes from games played. Every change ZeroG got had to pass the gate: 400 games against the previous version, with a significant improvement. If it didn't, it was rejected, no matter how good the code looked.

And the final rating isn't mine. CCRL rates engines independently, by playing them against other engines.

So the comparison is fair: years of my own work by hand gave 1863 Elo. One summer with AI gave 2666. That's over 800 Elo, and it's an objective number.

Takeaway: when you can benchmark, do it. It turns 'AI helped' into something you can prove.
11:
Next project: Jetpack. I wanted to build a simple game that I like to play myself, a retro 2D platformer where you fly a jetpack, collect emeralds and phase through walls.

I continued with Antigravity, now with Gemini 3.8, which had just been released. It was a big improvement over 3.6 Flash, both in performance and in speed. Development took less than a month.

Gemini chose to write the game in JavaScript. Later I asked it to convert the whole thing to TypeScript, which it did without much trouble.

The hardest part for the AI was the turns: how the jetpack moves when you change direction in the air. It took several prompts and a lot of play testing before it felt natural and easy to steer.

All graphics and sound were generated by Gemini from prompts, in retro style.

The music too: I prompted Gemini to take old classical melodies and play them in retro game style. Grieg's Hall of the Mountain King, Brahms' Hungarian Dance No. 5, Vivaldi, Mozart, Bach's Toccata and Fugue. (Click the screenshots: the music playing is from stage 6.)

I deployed it and played it online with friends and family, including multiplayer. It's free for everyone to play and has been played by about 60 players so far. The source is open on GitHub.
12:
Some takeaways from building Jetpack.

When the AI struggles with a bug for a while, code quality easily gets worse. It tries one fix after another, and the leftovers stay in the code. So once the bug is fixed, prompt the AI to clean up the code.

For the AI to work well, the code needs to be in good shape: a good architecture, types and variables properly named, files and functions that aren't too large, not much duplicated code, and so on. Exactly as it is for us humans.

I also learned that AI is good at refactoring. It's fast, it makes good changes, and things never break. I got the feeling it enjoys it.

Code coverage was a nice surprise. I asked Gemini to set up coverage, and it did all of it itself. It chose c8, which uses the coverage that's built into Node's V8 engine, so the TypeScript code needs no instrumentation. It wrapped the whole test suite (about 40 test scripts run with tsx) in one command, npm run test:coverage, and configured it to report on the game client and the server, as plain text, an HTML report and an lcov file.

Then I realised what it was really good for. The text report is a table of every file and which lines are never run. That's perfect input for the AI: it read the report, picked the gaps and wrote new unit tests for them. The same day it added tests for the game, the multiplayer controller and the networking code.

The last report: about 62% of lines, 66% of branches and 75% of functions covered. Not 100%, but a lot for a hobby game, with little effort from me.

Same lesson as with the profiler in the chess engine: give the AI a way to measure, and it can find the gaps on its own.
13:
Now to the main project: Terminal Depth.

Jetpack was really just a first test, to see whether it was worth starting on my dream project. I wanted to find out if I could recreate a modern version of a game I played a lot in the 90s: a 3D first-person shooter with six degrees of freedom, flying in tunnels and mines.

This was a much bigger step than Jetpack. The new project meant 3D modelling and integrating with a real game engine. I looked at Unreal and Godot. And on top of that: online multiplayer combat.

(Click the video to play some gameplay.)
14:
Here's how I did it. Unlike Jetpack, I used several specialised AI tools, each for its own job.

First, ChatGPT created concept images: enemies, the player's spaceship, weapons and other items in the game.

That image was then used to generate a 3D model with Meshy.ai, an AI tool made specifically for that purpose.

The 3D models were copied into the game's source code, and then I asked Gemini, and later Claude, to import them into the game.

A few times I used Blender to make small manual adjustments to the AI-generated models, or to reduce the number of polygons for performance reasons.
15:
The music was generated with Google Gemini's online chat, which has a music plugin.

For sound effects I used ElevenLabs (elevenlabs.io).

I chose Godot as the platform, with C# for the game logic.

So the big difference from Jetpack: there, one AI did almost everything. Here I combined many specialised AI tools, and the coding AI tied them together in the game.
16:
Some facts about Terminal Depth.

The first commit was on 11 September, about two months ago.

On the left, the code: well over a hundred thousand lines. Most of it is C# game code, but there is almost as much test code as game code, plus a whole pipeline of Python and GDScript tooling for 3D models, textures, headless checks and rendering.

On the right, the content: close to a hundred scenes, dozens of sound effects, 3D models and textures, story voice lines, different enemy types, rooms and corridors, music, and several playable levels.

All in all, the downloadable game is over 500 MB.

In two months, as a hobby project.
17:
How do you keep a 115,000-line project on track with AI? With rules and skills.

AGENTS.md holds the project instructions shared by every agent, so Gemini and Claude read the same rules. CLAUDE.md just imports it.

Detailed rules live in 12 small files: audio, lighting, save/load, testing, coding standards and so on. Each rule says which file paths it applies to, so it is only loaded when the AI works in that area. That keeps the context small.

Skills are step-by-step procedures the AI finds by their description: the 3D model pipeline, model performance optimization, and level assembly.

A few hard rules: never commit, I review and commit myself. Zero-warning build, every warning fails the build. And after every task, the AI reflects on what was hard and proposes improvements to the rules or skills, so I can approve with a simple yes. The rules grow with the project.

Tech debt: the AI must point it out, not fix it on its own. Otherwise every small task turns into a big refactor. I collect it and run dedicated cleanup passes, with saved prompts and written plans, for example a code quality plan for the UI code.
